opus-5.5.text:
I think the case is actually pretty strong, and it's stronger than people sometimes give it credit for. The intuition a lot of people have is that coding and robotics are these totally different things: one is symbolic, abstract, lives on a computer, and the other is about torques and contact forces and getting your fingers around a coffee mug. So why would you want one model doing both?

But if you look at what's made the big language models work, it's not that they're specialized for any one task. It's that they've absorbed this enormous amount of structure about the world, about how problems decompose, about how people reason through things. And a lot of that is exactly what a robot needs. When a robot is cleaning up a kitchen, the hard part often isn't the low-level motor control by itself. It's knowing that the dish goes in the sink before the sponge comes out, that if the drawer is stuck you try something different, that a spill means you should grab a towel. That's common-sense reasoning and planning, and it's the same kind of thing that shows up when you're debugging a program: you form a hypothesis, try something, look at the result, and adjust.

The other side of it, which I find even more interesting, is that the transfer can go the other way too. Physical interaction is a very grounded form of experience. You get immediate, unambiguous feedback from the world. In the long run I suspect that kind of grounding helps a model's general understanding, in the same way that people's abstract reasoning is built on top of a lot of embodied experience.

Practically speaking, the way we've approached this is to start from a vision-language model that already knows a lot about the world and then teach it to output actions. What we've seen is that the knowledge carries over. The robot can follow instructions it's never seen in the robot data, recognize objects it's never manipulated, and generalize to new homes. That's a strong hint that a shared representation is doing real work.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are real tensions. Robots need to run in real time, at high frequency, with very precise continuous outputs, and that's a different regime from generating tokens for a code completion. So there are real architectural questions about how you get one system that can think slowly and deliberately when it needs to and react quickly when it needs to. People sometimes frame this as System 1 versus System 2, and I think that's roughly the right picture. But those feel like engineering problems rather than fundamental barriers.

So my view is that the endpoint is probably something like one foundation model that understands the world broadly and can express that understanding through whatever interface it's given, whether that's a keyboard or a robot arm. The question is less whether that's possible and more how we get the data and the training recipes to get there.

r001.rationale: The response calls the case for one model “pretty strong” and explains how shared reasoning and knowledge can benefit robotics, supporting the idea that the benefits justify a combined model.

r002.rationale: It describes coding as symbolic and abstract, but does not characterize programming as the pinnacle of abstract knowledge work.

r003.rationale: It says people view coding as abstract, but does not attribute difficulty with programming to that abstractness.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the case is actually pretty strong, and it's strong for a reason that's a little bit subtle. If you look at how we got to where we are with language models, a big part of the story is that there's some kind of shared substrate. Learning to write code didn't just make the models better at writing code, it made them better at reasoning, at planning, at decomposing problems into steps. The skills that you acquire from one domain turn out to be more general than the domain itself.

Now, robotics is interesting because, on the surface, it looks very different. You're dealing with continuous control, with physics, with the messiness of the real world. But when you actually think about what a robot needs to do to accomplish a complex task, it needs to figure out what the goal is, break it down into subgoals, figure out what to do when something goes wrong, recover from mistakes. Those are exactly the capabilities that you get from training on things like code and language and math. So there's a very natural argument that a model which already understands how to reason about the world and about procedures should have a big head start when it comes to acting in the world.

The other direction is maybe less obvious but I think equally important. Right now, language models learn about the physical world secondhand. They read about it. They never actually have to deal with the consequences of being wrong about physics. A model that has to actually act in the world gets grounded in a way that a text-only model never does. It learns what it means for something to be heavy, for something to break, for an action to be irreversible. And I would bet that kind of grounding improves the model's understanding in ways that show up even in domains that have nothing to do with robots.

So the way I'd frame it is: it's not just that one model can do both. It's that the two kinds of experience are complementary. The reasoning and abstraction you get from code and language make the robot more capable, and the grounding you get from the robot makes the reasoning more real.

Now, the practical challenge, and this is where I think a lot of the real work is, is that the data regimes are wildly different. There's a nearly unlimited supply of text and code on the internet. There's very little robot data, and what exists is expensive and slow to collect. So the question of whether a single model is the right answer in practice is really a question of whether the transfer is good enough that the robot data can be small, and whether we can design training procedures where the robot side benefits from the scale on the language side rather than getting drowned out by it. My sense is that we're seeing early evidence that this works, that vision-language-action models that start from strong pretrained backbones really do inherit a lot of useful knowledge. But we're still in the early innings of figuring out how to do this well.

r001.rationale: The response calls the case for one model doing both “pretty strong” and says code and language reasoning give a robot a “big head start.”

r002.rationale: It discusses programming’s transferable reasoning benefits but does not characterize programming as the pinnacle of abstract knowledge work.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss why people find programming difficult or attribute that difficulty to programming’s abstract nature.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty compelling case for it. Writing code and controlling a robot look like very different tasks at the level of the outputs, but a lot of the underlying capabilities you want are shared. You need to reason about what will happen if you take some action, break a problem down into pieces, and recover when something doesn’t work.

Suppose you ask a robot to clean up the kitchen. Some of that task is physical control, but some of it is figuring out what you mean by clean, where things belong, and which steps depend on other steps. It would be very useful if the system doing that could draw on the same knowledge that lets it answer questions or write a program.

The harder question is whether training on those things actually improves its ability to act. Having a model that can talk intelligently about grasping doesn’t necessarily mean it can grasp something. It needs experience with the physical world and feedback about whether its actions worked. So I’d distinguish the case for sharing knowledge and representations, which I think is quite strong, from the claim that you can get robotics simply by training a sufficiently good language or coding model.

And a single model doesn’t necessarily mean that every motor command has to go through the same computation that you use to solve a programming problem. You could have a unified system with different components operating at different timescales. The important question is how much useful transfer you get, rather than whether you can call the whole thing one model.

r001.rationale: The response says code writing and robotics share useful capabilities and argues that a unified system could bring programming-related knowledge to robot tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize computer programming as the pinnacle of abstract knowledge work.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute people’s difficulty with programming to programming’s abstract nature.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty compelling case for it, but it depends on what you mean by a single model. If you mean that exactly the same network, with exactly the same inputs and outputs, should control a robot’s motors and write Python, that’s not obviously the right design. But if you mean a shared model that can draw on knowledge from both domains, then I think there are very good reasons to want that.

A lot of robotics problems are actually reasoning problems. If I ask a robot to clean up a kitchen, it has to figure out what needs to happen, in what order, and what to do when something goes wrong. Being able to write code is one way of expressing that kind of structured reasoning. And the knowledge you acquire from working with language and code can be useful even if the final action is physical.

The harder question is how much transfer you get in the other direction. Does learning to interact with the physical world make you better at writing code? I think that’s plausible, because interaction gives you a way to learn about consequences: you make a prediction, take an action, and find out whether you were right. But I wouldn’t take it for granted. You have to demonstrate that the joint training actually helps.

So I would expect some shared foundation, with different mechanisms for producing actions in different settings. The important thing is that the robot can use the model’s broader knowledge while still learning the physical skills that you can’t get just by reading about them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there are very good reasons for a shared model and that knowledge from language and code can help with robotics, supporting the case that code capabilities may justify a model spanning both.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses code as a way to express structured reasoning but does not characterize programming as the pinnacle of abstract knowledge work.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not explain people's difficulty with programming or attribute it to programming's abstract nature.
